body_markdown:
I bought a 1979 International Scout II sight-unseen on eBay in 2024 and owned it for just over 16 months. Before my ownership, it had spent the majority of its life in the warm and relatively dry climate of Medford, Oregon. The sun is hotter and sharper in southern Oregon than it is in the northern Willamette Valley where I live. Up here, the paint is usually fine on these rigs, and it’s the body that’s shot due to the humidity. So, to find a sun-patinaed Scout II like this one was delightfully unusual.


This example was sun-beaten to perfection, with large swaths of the formerly gray-metallic green paint either faded to a light gray or else burnt completely off the body, leaving surface-rusted panels accented by the factory white side graphics.


Nick Jaynes


Nick Jaynes


Nick Jaynes


Nick Jaynes


Funnily enough, I bought this Scout II within a week of buying my[1976 Scout Traveler](https://www.hagerty.com/valuation-tools/international_(ihc)/scout_traveler/1976) . I thought that I’d drive and enjoy the Scout II while I rebuilt the Traveler—a brilliant combo. I’d still get to enjoy a summer with a vintage 4×4 while restoring a second.


A shipping company delivered the Scout II, and it quickly became apparent that, even though I’d spoken to the seller on the phone, I hadn’t gotten the whole story. While the body was in relatively good condition and only needed minor rust repairs (compared to my Traveler), the drivetrain, brakes, suspension, and steering were either shot or extremely worn out.


Make no mistake: Patina princesses are 100% worth buying. You just have to understand what you’re getting yourself into, and you must have realistic goals for what they can be and how much achieving those goals will cost you in both blood and treasure.


## Worn Out


Nick Jaynes


Steering the ’79 Scout II was like piloting a riverboat. Wheel inputs, made in huge arcs, were mere suggestions for the front end. Saw it left to right in 90- to 180-degree swings, and it the thing was happy to just … keep going straight. At first, it was amusing, until I imagined a wayward child darting in front of me.


Unlike my Traveler, which has a manual transmission, the Scout II was fitted from the factory with a Chrysler-sourced 727 TorqueFlite. It slipped, shuddered, and shook more than it shifted. It was a three-speed, I think? For months, until I had the transmission rebuilt, I didn’t truly know for sure. How much horsepower the 345-cubic-inch V-8 was producing through its worn-out two-barrel carburetor was anyone’s guess, because the TorqueFlite zapped most of it.


Nick Jaynes


Nick Jaynes


The brakes were just as frightening as the steering. They retarded forward momentum about as well as a handkerchief might, if you held it out the window in the shape of a parachute. Though, to be fair, the right front brake caliper grabbed pretty well, darting the truck with great expediency to the right-hand curb. So, at least there was that. Nevermind what the steering did; I knew that if I needed to, in a pinch, I could send the truck rightward with the brake pedal.


The suspension was brutally stiff, too, slamming you into the battered bucket seats at the slightest roadway imperfection. If that weren’t painful enough, some joker had replaced the headliner with white-painted pegboard. It leapt up and down and slammed side to side over bumps and around corners, adding auditory injury to the insulting suspension. I like to think of it as the soundtrack to spinal stenosis.


## Mr. Popular


Nick Jaynes


From the outside, you couldn’t tell any of this, of course. When I drove the truck through town, men—mostly dads in their 40s and 50s—would stop what they were doing, be it walking with their wife and kids or enjoying a pasta dinner at an outdoor bistro, and run up to the truck. Beaming, they would congratulate me on how cool the Scout II was. Never have I ever had more people compliment me or my truck than I did when piloting that Scout II patina princess. I am still not quite sure what, exactly, tickled the fancy of middle-aged men in Portland. It was a neat-looking truck, sure. But was it neat enough to elicit such an enthusiastic response? I wasn’t convinced.


At the outset, the reception I received when I drove the Scout II outweighed the fear and physical agony I felt driving it. After a few short weeks, however, I broke and decided to have a professional vintage car shop make it slightly more roadworthy.


Since I was busy running my business during the day and[rebuilding the Traveler](https://www.hagerty.com/media/opinion/what-a-13-month-scout-rebuild-taught-me/) in my dad’s barn on nights and weekends, I farmed out the mechanical work. Little did I know that I wouldn’t see the Scout II again for five months, and that retrieving it would come with an $11,000 bill. That didn’t include the $2600 TorqueFlite rebuild, which I had done at the only transmission shop in Portland that would touch a vehicle built prior to 1995, or the new Holley two-barrel carb I acquired and installed myself.


Nick Jaynes


Nick Jaynes


Nick Jaynes


By the time I got the Scout II back, driving and braking straight, winter was fast approaching, so it sat mostly untouched in my suburban garage until spring. Once the Pacific Northwest thawed out in 2025, I swapped the Traveler for the Scout II in my father’s barn and patched a few minor rust holes. The hardest part, I was surprised to discover, was removing what remained of the factory blue carpet. The carpet was further evidence of the truck’s working life; I found plenty of nails beneath it. I replaced it with an oxblood-red carpet kit that I thought accented the faded exterior better than royal blue did.


I eventually sold the Scout II for less than I had in it. That was a bummer, sure. But, by then, I was glad to have it gone and to get some of the money I’d invested back into my pocket. After all, by that time the Traveler was back on the road with a fresh 345 V-8 and floorboards to match.


## Ooh La La


Nick Jaynes


If my experience with the Scout II weren’t enough of a cautionary tale, let me give you some advice on patina princesses. To quote the 1973 song “Ooh La La” by Faces, “I wish that I knew what I know now.”


First off, as they say about human relationships, don’t fall in love with a face.[Patina is all the rage](https://www.hagerty.com/media/opinion/auto-anthro-the-power-of-patina/) in classic cars right now. I get the appeal. Anyone can get a rig restored to like-new condition, but a car can only be weather-beaten for 50 years once, and that has real cachet. What’s more, patinaed cars offer less to worry about. If yours picks up a dent or a scratch, it’s just one more chapter in the car’s story.


However, that patina is more often than not indicative of abuse, misuse, or neglect, and the interior and mechanical components will likely be in the same worse-for-wear condition.


Nick Jaynes


Nick Jaynes


Nick Jaynes


[As I have written before,](https://www.hagerty.com/media/buying-and-selling/tips-for-buying-an-old-car-sight-unseen-without-getting-torched/) get your patina princess inspected by an unbiased third party, be it a mechanically inclined friend or a mechanic versed in classic cars.


With that inspection in hand, research parts availability and cost. No one sells an off-the-shelf rebuilt steering box for the Scout II anymore (not one I could find, anyhow) or the hydraulic hoses that accompany it. So, mine had to be rebuilt by hand and the hoses custom-made. If I’d known that before I bought it, I would have made different choices with my timeline and budget. Ditto the TorqueFlite. Who would have thought that a transmission produced by the millions would have sunk to the untouchable caste with bits of unobtanium inside? Not me.


I still want you to fall in love with a patina princess. I want you to buy it, fix it up a bit, and enjoy it. But don’t for one second think you’ll find a well-preserved, tight-as-a-drum drivetrain beneath a delightfully crusty paint job.


All those dads who abandoned their pasta to admire my Scout II only ever saw the paint. I’m the one who had to drive it home.
